Espousal
es-POW-zul
n.
From Old French espouser, “to betroth, marry,” from Latin sponsare (to promise solemnly). Renders the Hebrew k’lūlāh (betrothal, espousal—Jer 2:2), and the Greek mnēsteuō-family (to betroth) and harmozō (to join, betroth—2 Cor 11:2).

Biblical Definition

Espousal in Scripture is the covenant promise of marriage preceding consummation—the binding pledge between bride and bridegroom that, in biblical-and-ancient-Near-Eastern usage, was as binding as marriage itself though preceding the wedding. The Hebrew k’lūlāh appears at one of the most tender places in the prophets: thus saith the LORD; I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown (Jer 2:2). The LORD looks back upon Israel’s early covenantal-honeymoon period in the wilderness, when she loved Him with the fresh devotion of a newly-espoused bride, and grieves over her present unfaithfulness against that love. Hosea takes up the same theme: and I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD. The LORD’s betrothal of His people is anchored in His own attributes—righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness, mercies, faithfulness—and is the substantive ground of His covenant fidelity even when His people’s is broken. The New Testament continues the figure. Mary is espoused to Joseph at the time of the incarnation (Matt 1:18; Luke 1:27; 2:5); the binding character of biblical espousal is what makes Joseph’s discovery of her pregnancy a serious matter requiring formal action even though they had not yet come together (Matt 1:19). Paul gives the figure ecclesial application: I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ (2 Cor 11:2-3). The church is presently in the espousal period—betrothed to Christ, awaiting the marriage of the Lamb—and the pastoral concern of the apostle is the chastity of the espoused bride during the betrothal interval, the keeping of her faithful to her one husband until the day of the wedding. Espousal is therefore the theological category that names the church’s present age: she is not yet at the wedding, but she is no less truly bound to Christ; the consummation awaits, but the betrothal is real, and the discipline of the espousal period is fidelity to the Bridegroom amid the temptations of the unbelieving world.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ESPOUSAL as the act of espousing or betrothing; the act of contracting persons for marriage; in scripture, the binding covenant promise of marriage between bridegroom and bride preceding the consummation.

expand to see more

ESPOUSAL, n. — 1. The act of espousing or betrothing. 2. The act of contracting persons for marriage; a contract or mutual promise of marriage. 3. Adoption; protection. The love of thine espousals (Jer 2:2).

ESPOUSE, v.t. — 1. To betroth; to promise or engage in marriage by contract in writing or by some pledge. 2. To take in marriage; to marry. 3. To embrace; to adopt; to take to one’s self with a view to maintain.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 2:2 — "I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown."

Hosea 2:19-20 — "And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD."

2 Corinthians 11:2 — "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ."

Matthew 1:18 — "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

Modern Corruption

The doctrine of espousal is corrupted by the contemporary collapse of marriage’s covenantal binding character—in which engagement is treated as easily dissoluble and even marriage itself is held provisionally—and by the loss of the ecclesial application that names the present age as the church’s espousal period requiring her chastity to her one Husband.

expand to see more

The contemporary collapse of marriage’s covenantal binding character has eroded the very category Scripture means by espousal. Engagement is treated as easily dissoluble—a try-out for marriage that can be exited at will; even marriage itself is held provisionally—a commitment subject to the parties’ ongoing satisfaction. In this register the biblical espousal—a binding covenant promise that was as serious as marriage itself—is nearly unintelligible. The recovery is the recovery of the covenantal seriousness Scripture assigns to the binding promises men and women make to one another and to the LORD they invoke. Engagement is not a try-out; biblical marriage is not provisional; the covenants of God’s people are real, binding, and meant to image the deeper covenant between Christ and His church.

The companion corruption is the loss of the ecclesial application of the doctrine. The present age is the church’s espousal period: she is betrothed to Christ, awaiting the marriage of the Lamb, called by her apostle to keep herself a chaste virgin to her one Husband amid the temptations of the surrounding unbelieving world. Where this ecclesial-eschatological framing is lost, the church easily drifts into the spiritual adultery against which Scripture so urgently warns: friendship with the world that James calls enmity with God; the love of the world that John condemns; the spiritual fornication the prophets thunder against. Recover the doctrine, and the church recovers also the discipline of the espousal interval: fidelity to her Bridegroom amid every cultural pressure, the simplicity that is in Christ against every Eve-style beguilement, and the eager anticipation of the wedding-day at the end of the present age. I am jealous over you with godly jealousy—Paul’s apostolic concern is the standing pastoral concern for every congregation in the espousal age.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew k’lūlāh (espousal—Jer 2:2) and ’āras (to betroth, Hos 2:19-20); Greek mnēsteuō (to betroth—Matt 1:18; Luke 1:27; 2:5) and harmozō (to join, betroth—2 Cor 11:2)—the binding covenant promise of marriage preceding consummation, applied ecclesially to the church’s present age awaiting the marriage of the Lamb.

expand to see more

Hebrew k’lūlāh (H3623) — espousal, betrothal (Jer 2:2).

Hebrew ’āras (H781) — to betroth (Hos 2:19-20; Deut 20:7; 22:23-29).

Greek mnēsteuō (G3423) — to betroth (Matt 1:18; Luke 1:27; 2:5).

Greek harmozō (G718) — to join, fit together, betroth (2 Cor 11:2).

Usage

"I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals—the LORD’s tender recollection of Israel’s honeymoon-period devotion in the wilderness."

"I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ—Paul names the present age as the church’s espousal interval requiring her fidelity."

"Contemporary collapse of binding covenant erodes the espousal category; recovery is the recovery of the covenantal seriousness of marriage and of the church’s discipline as bride during the present age."
